title: Anim2DClear
question: How does 2D animation work?
hook: Every cartoon is a pile of drawings. Flip a flip-book, fill in a jump between key poses, switch the 12 principles on and off on a bouncing ball, spread cels out under a multiplane camera, and make a mango-headed kid talk.

explainer.title: A flip-book made big
explainer.text: A cartoon is thousands of still drawings, each a little different, shown one after another. Cinema shows 24 frames a second; most hand-drawn animation holds each drawing for two frames, “on twos”, so one character needs 12 drawings a second, 720 a minute.

explainer.title: Keys first, in-betweens after
explainer.text: The key animator draws the poses that tell the story. An in-betweener fills the gaps, following a timing chart whose ticks bunch near a key where the move slows in or out. A light table, or onion skinning in software, shows the drawings before and after.

explainer.title: Twelve principles
explainer.text: Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston’s The Illusion of Life (1981) lists the 12 principles: squash and stretch, anticipation, staging, straight ahead and pose to pose, follow-through, slow in and out, arcs, secondary action, timing, exaggeration, solid drawing and appeal. A bouncing ball shows most of them, and its timing shows its weight.

explainer.title: Cels, backgrounds and depth
explainer.text: From 1914, moving characters were inked and painted on clear cels over one painted background. Disney’s multiplane camera (1937) spread the art over levels of glass, so near levels slide faster than far ones when the camera moves: parallax. A model sheet keeps every artist’s drawings on model.

explainer.title: Rigs, tweens and curves
explainer.text: On a computer, you can still draw every frame, or build a cut-out rig of pieces on pivots. You key the poses on a timeline and the computer tweens the in-betweens, spaced by an easing curve: straight is robotic, an S-curve eases in and out.

explainer.title: Making drawings talk
explainer.text: The voice is recorded first and read frame by frame onto an exposure sheet. Each frame gets a mouth shape from a small chart, often a frame or two ahead of the sound. Acting, a head tilt, raised brows or a blink, is what makes it feel alive.

concepts.def: One still picture in a film; cinema shows 24 a second.
Each drawing held for two frames: 12 drawings a second.
A main drawing that shows an important moment of an action.
A drawing that fills the gap between two keys.
Faint ghosts of the drawings before and after the one you are drawing.
Flattening on impact and stretching in fast motion, keeping the same volume.
A clear sheet with the character inked on the front and painted on the back.
Artwork on levels at different distances from the camera, for parallax and depth.
In-betweens calculated by the computer between two keyframes.
A chart with one row per frame, listing sounds, actions and drawings.
